newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania Socialists aim to form gov't by July 25.
newsitem.headline: Albania Socialists aim to form gov't by July 25.

text.p: Albania's ex-communist Socialists said on Monday they hoped to form a new government by July 25 after winning a landslide victory in elections called to end months of violence and bloodshed in Europe's poorest country.

After two rounds of voting, the Socialists and their leftist allies looked set for a two-thirds majority over President Sali Berisha's right-wing Democratic Party, enabling them to pass radical laws and replace the head of state.

Socialist leader Fatos Nano, who has said he will be prime minister of the coalition government, said he hoped to convene parliament by July 20 and form a government by July 25 even though a few districts have to go to a third vote next Sunday.

"There is no third round but only a runoff in one or two zones, something which does not hamper the new parliament to be convened in a plenary session as soon as possible," Nano told reporters on Monday.
"I think the Democrats and President Berisha have understood and will cooperate to carry that out."

The early election was called in March after the collapse of popular savings funds triggered a violent rebellion and over 1,500 deaths, forcing the Democratic government to resign after five years of ruling the Balkan nation.
The Socialists won over 80 of 155 seats in the first vote eight days ago, ousting the Democrats who were blamed for allowing the shady pyramid schemes to flourish.
A total of 34 seats where no candidate won a majority returned to the polls last Sunday but voter turnout was low as interest waned in the wake of the Socialists' victory.
Final results from the runoff ballots were yet to come but early numbers showed the Socialists had won 12 of 17 seats where results had been finalised.

International monitors from the Organisation of Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) and Council of Europe had described the first round in Albania's fourth multi-party election since the 1990 fall of communism as "adequate".
"The second round was generally satisfactory," said OSCE spokeswoman Catherine Lalumiere, who will release an OSCE report on the election in Warsaw on Tuesday.
"This election...will allow the international community to unblock the aid for this country."

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has been waiting for a new government before negotiating terms of an economic reform programme. The IMF has disbursed some $60 million in credits to Albania since 1992 but the programme was suspended in 1995.
The elections passed off relatively smoothly in a country that has been under gun rule for months. There were five deaths reported during the two votes but not all were election related.
During the first vote, an election official at Fier in southern Albania was shot dead in a polling station.

On Sunday four were killed. The Albanian news agency ATA reported two people were killed and one seriously injured, dying later, when a man opened fire in a polling booth near Shkoder in northern Albania. The first victims were said to be the gunman's uncle and cousin.
Later on Sunday, a police officer was killed in a shootout at a village in the Kruje district, just outside Tirana.
The first major political casualty was Democratic Party chairman Tritan Shehu, who announced he was stepping down on Monday after securing under 30 percent in Sunday's runoff.

This seemed to open the way for Berisha to take over as party leader and fill one of the Democrats' 10 assembly seats, allocated under a system of proportional representation, when he resigns or is voted out as president by the new parliament.

As the new government prepared to take over, Albania's self-proclaimed king Leka I vowed to continue his fight to restore the monarchy despite rejection of the idea in a referendum on June 29 that showed 66 percent opposition.
"I don't believe the vote has gone against it," Leka told Reuters in an interview on Monday. "I can't give up, I have the trust of so many people."
With the election sealed, Italy's Defence Chief of Staff, Admiral Guido Venturoni, said a 7,000-strong multinational security force in Albania would withdraw by August 12.
The 11-nation Italian-led force was deployed in April to guard the distribution of aid and secure elections in Albania.
